summary: DNS translates names such as www.example.com into IP addresses through a hierarchy of servers. A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which walks the hierarchy from the root down and caches the answers.

sections.heading: The hierarchy
sections.body: Names are read right to left: root (.), top-level domain (com), second-level (example), host (www). Each level is a zone served by authoritative name servers that delegate to the next level with NS records (RFC 1035).

sections.heading: Resolution walk
sections.body: For a cold cache the recursive resolver performs iterative queries:
sections.code:
1. Client -> recursive resolver: www.example.com A?
2. Resolver -> root server: referral to .com TLD servers
3. Resolver -> .com TLD server: referral to example.com name servers
4. Resolver -> example.com authoritative: A 93.184.216.34, TTL 3600
5. Resolver caches it and answers the client

sections.heading: Message format
sections.body: A DNS message has a 12-byte header (ID, flags, and four counts) followed by Question, Answer, Authority, and Additional sections. Flags include QR (query/response), AA (authoritative), TC (truncated), RD (recursion desired), RA (recursion available), and RCODE.
bullets: The ID matches responses to queries.
Names are sequences of length-prefixed labels, and may be compressed with 2-byte pointers to earlier occurrences.
Resource records have NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH, RDATA.

sections.heading: Record types
bullets: NS: authoritative name server for a zone.
CNAME: alias to a canonical name.
MX: mail exchanger with a preference.
PTR: reverse lookup from address to name.

sections.heading: Transport
sections.body: DNS uses UDP port 53 for normal queries and TCP port 53 for zone transfers and when responses are truncated (TC bit). The original UDP limit was 512 bytes; EDNS0 (RFC 6891) lets clients advertise larger buffers.
Every record carries a TTL telling resolvers how long to cache it. Caching, including negative caching of NXDOMAIN (RFC 2308), absorbs most queries; lowering a TTL before a migration speeds failover.
A stub resolver asks for a complete answer (recursive query). The resolver then queries servers iteratively, following referrals. Authoritative servers normally do not recurse for outsiders.
DNSSEC signs records (RRSIG), publishes keys (DNSKEY), and chains trust from the root through DS records, letting validators detect forged answers. It authenticates data but does not encrypt queries.
DNS over TLS (RFC 7858, port 853) and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) hide queries from on-path observers.
`dig +trace example.com` shows the delegation walk; `dig @8.8.8.8 example.com MX` queries a specific server; `dig -x 8.8.8.8` does a reverse lookup.

takeaways: DNS is a hierarchy: root, TLD, domain, host; NS records delegate.
Resolvers cache by TTL; a cold lookup walks root -> TLD -> authoritative.
UDP/53 normally, TCP/53 for large responses and zone transfers.
